content: The primary goal of cystic fibrosis treatment is to reduce lung inflammation. Inhaled corticosteroids are frequently used for this purpose in both children and adults with cystic fibrosis. These medications are thought to potentially reduce lung damage caused by inflammation and alleviate symptoms such as wheezing. However, it is crucial to evaluate the current evidence regarding the risks and benefits of inhaled corticosteroids, particularly given their known adverse effects on growth. This review is an update of a previously published analysis, but due to the limited research in this area, further updates are not anticipated. The objective of this review was to determine the effectiveness of regular use of inhaled corticosteroids compared to not using them in individuals with cystic fibrosis. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group Trials Register, which includes references from electronic databases, hand-searched journals, and conference abstracts. Additional information was requested from pharmaceutical companies producing inhaled corticosteroids and from authors of identified trials. The most recent search was conducted on November 19, 2018. The review included randomized or quasi-randomized trials, both published and unpublished, that compared inhaled corticosteroids to placebo or standard treatment in people with cystic fibrosis. Two independent reviewers assessed the methodological quality and risk of bias in the trials using established criteria. Data were extracted using standardized forms, and the quality of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE criteria. The search identified 35 citations, of which 27 (representing 13 trials) met the inclusion criteria. These 13 trials involved 525 participants with cystic fibrosis, aged between 6 and 55 years. One of the trials was a withdrawal study involving 171 individuals who were already using inhaled corticosteroids. The methodological quality and risk of bias were challenging to assess due to incomplete information in the published reports. Most trials reported objective measures of airway function, but the data were often incomplete and collected at varying time points. The trials did not demonstrate any significant differences in forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) or forced vital capacity (FVC) as a percentage of predicted values. However, the quality of the evidence was low due to risks of bias and the small number of participants. It remains uncertain whether inhaled corticosteroids improve exercise tolerance, bronchial hyperreactivity, or the frequency of exacerbations, as the evidence quality was very low. Data from one trial suggested that inhaled corticosteroids may have little to no impact on quality of life, but this conclusion is based on low-quality evidence. Three trials reported adverse effects, but the evidence was of low quality, making it unclear whether inhaled corticosteroids increase the risk of adverse effects. However, one study indicated that high doses of inhaled corticosteroids negatively affected growth. In conclusion, the evidence from these trials is of low to very low quality and is insufficient to determine whether inhaled corticosteroids are beneficial for individuals with cystic fibrosis. Withdrawal of inhaled corticosteroids in those already using them has been shown to be safe. There is some evidence suggesting that these medications may cause harm, particularly in terms of growth. It remains uncertain whether long-term use of inhaled corticosteroids reduces lung inflammation and improves survival, and it is unlikely that this question will be definitively answered through randomized controlled trials.
